title: Machine learning-based plasma proteomic analysis identifies a novel disease-defining biomarkers
projectDescription: Recent advances in serum proteomic analysis tools have expanded our understanding of various diseases. To identify a novel disease-specific proteomic markers, we used the high-throughput proximity extension assay (PEA) platform to profile plasma proteins from 62 patients with atopic dermatitis (AD), or ulcerative colitis (UC) and 29 healthy subjects. Differentially expressed protein (DEP) analysis yielded 85 (20 unique) and 99 (14 unique) upregulated proteins in AD and UC, respectively, compared to healthy subjects. We integrated a machine-learning (ML) model and selected 24 proteins to distinguish between the diseases, which accurately predicted disease-defining biomarkers based on distinctive proteomic signatures and disease severity. Correlation analysis with disease severity identified upregulated ML-selected proteins such as CCL13, CCL26, CD70, CDON, LY6D and MMP1 in AD, and ITM2A and REG4 in UC. Among these identified proteins, we suggest CDON, CD70 and LY6D, which had highly correlated expression levels, as AD-specific biomarkers. Thus, our results provide insight into the application of ML algorithms for disease diagnosis, and our model may be expanded to other disease contexts.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Sample collection and plasma isolation All blood was obtained from each donor using heparin CPT tubes (cat No. 362753, BD Vacutainer®, Becton Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, US). Blood processing occurred within two hours, involving 20 minutes of centrifugation at 1,800 × g at room temperature (RT). The resulting plasma was transferred to Eppendorf 1.5 ml tubes and stored at -80°C until processing.  Proteomic profiling The study analyzed 91 samples from the 3 cohorts using the Olink 384 Inflammatory I panel (1188, v4.0, 2024-04-16) shown in Supplementary File 1: Table S1. Samples were randomly assigned in the 384-well plate with three quality controls including sample, negative and plate control to minimize variability and batch effects. Olink performed PEA involves paired oligonucleotide antibodies that bind in proximity enables multiplex protein screening. The DNA hybridization creates a PCR target sequence confirming the specificity of target of proteins. Once it finished, NGS were performed to detect target sequences in which proteins are quantified. The NGS readout generates normalized protein expression (NPX) on an arbitrary log2 scale in which higher NPX means high protein concentration. The median of NPX were compared to all aligned assay medians for intensity normalization. Also, the limit of detection (LOD) was calculated three times the standard deviation (SD) to evaluate the contamination through background signals.
dataProcessingProtocol: Statistical analysis The Mann-Whitney U test was conducted at a confidence level of 0.95 to analyze total proteins comparing the disease and healthy controls. Following the initial DEP analysis, DEPs were filtered for multiple correction testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. And adjusted P-value of more than 0.01 and log2 Fold Change (FC) of 0.5 was considered indicative of disease-associated proteins among all significant DEPs (Supplementary File 2: Table S2 and Table S3). Bioinformatics analysis of DEPs was performed using GraphPad Prism (9.5.1). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using the PCA function in OlinkAnalyze package (4.0.2) and did not exclude any proteins and samples in Supplementary File 1: Fig. S1.  Pearson correlation was used to assess the linear relationship for upregulated proteins within each disease cohort using Python version 3.11.3. The algorithm computed the p-values of the correlation matrix for each protein positioned on the x- and y-axes can be found in Supplementary File 2: Table S4 and Table S5. Correlation of severity scores with protein expression level with 95% confidence interval for both axes utilized simple regression model using GraphPad Prism (9.5.1) shown in Supplementary File 1: Fig. S2 and Fig. S3.  Machine learning model A disease prediction model was developed to identify disease-specific proteins using logistic regression with LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) penalization. The study cohort comprised 91 patient samples, which were divided into a training set of 63 patients and a test set of 28 patients. A total of 136 DEPs were used as features in the model. The regularization hyperparameter of the LASSO model, λ, was determined to be 1 by 5-fold cross-validation. Proteins with non-zero coefficients in the LASSO regression model were selected as biomarker candidates, and 24 proteins were selected for use in the final predictive model. An independent set of tests was then used to evaluate the performance of the model through metrics such as area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. Disease-specific protein modules were also assessed its performance to distinguished from each disease and healthy controls. The ML analysis were performed using scikit-learn version 1.2.2 in Python 3.10.10.
